First, to the National, where The House of Bernarda Alba has had a makeover in Rebecca Frecknall’s desolately powerful production of Lorca’s tragedy.

But the triumph in this new version of the Frederick Garcia Lorca classic belongs to the women behind the scenes. In her first new stage work since the pandemic, the toweringly gifted playwright Alice Birch has spliced Lorca’s original with some of the radical stylings of her 2017 masterpiece ‘Anatomy of a Suicide’.

It presents a world that we scrutinise without entering, and lives that we observe to be intolerable without ever feeling especially moved. Merle Hensel’s set is a white dolls’ house. A rifle hangs on the wall of the sitting room, a crucifix over each bed.

As Bernarda Alba, Harriet Walter opens the action standing in front of the dolls house structure, watchful and wary, listening to the murmurs from within. She cuts an imposing figure, bolt upright, feet planted firmly on the ground.
